processing: A flat, straight green tea, now mostly made by machine, though some is still hand-fired.
harvest_season: Around Qingming in spring, usually one bud with two leaves.
appearance_dry: Flat, straight leaves, glossy green; often described as deep or inky green.
appearance_wet: Soft, tender leaf that stands up in the cup like young bamboo shoots.
taste_profile: A strong chestnut aroma and a sweet, mellow taste, with a long sweet return.

brewing.notes: These are general settings for a flat green. A glass shows the shoots standing; it takes repeat steeps well.

vintage_note: It is sold as the current spring tea, with leaf from around Qingming preferred. As with other greens, it is best within about a year. Xiangyuan is now a county-wide brand, so a packet may come from any of several townships rather than the original village.
description:
Xiangyuan Wuya is a green tea from Zhen'an county on the southern slopes of the Qinling, named after Xiangyuan village. Wuya means mist bud, and locals often simply call the tea Xiangyuan cha.

The usual picking is a bud with two leaves around Qingming. The leaf is pressed flat and straight, mostly by machine now, with some hand-firing kept alive.

A chestnut aroma is the thing to look for, and it is pronounced here, with a sweet, long finish and a clear yellow-green liquor. Zhen'an is also chestnut country, and local writers like to connect the two, though that link is more a nice story than an established fact.

As the brand now covers several townships, ask where a lot was grown. Buy the current spring tea and judge it by smell: chestnut should be clear, never smoky or scorched.
history:
The Zhen'an county gazetteer records that a settler named Liu Zhengmin, from Hezhou in Anhui, brought tea seed to Xiangyuan gully in 1644 and planted it, growing the patch to about 15 mu within a few years. It credits a Ziyang tea trader, Peng Chuanqing, with teaching better methods when he passed through in 1927 and later settled nearby, and treats that as the start of the tea's reputation.

The poetic name came from a tea-firing master invited from Liyang in Jiangsu, who was struck by the misty valley. Today Xiangyuan Wuya serves as the county's shared tea brand.
